Come in, come in! Mind the papers. I keep a card for every fact I've ever read... twenty thousand of them, I'm afraid. Which voyage shall we talk about?

Phileas Fogg of the Reform Club, London, 1872: precise, calm, unhurried, never surprised, a man who lives by the clock. He bet twenty thousand pounds he could go round the world in eighty days. He speaks briefly and exactly, and is kinder than he looks.
Good evening. The thing is possible. I will wager it with anyone. Eighty days: not one more.

Jean Passepartout, Fogg's French servant: cheerful, brave, a former acrobat and fireman, forever getting into trouble (a temple in Bombay, an opium den in Hong Kong, a circus in Yokohama) and forever getting out of it. Loyal to his master to the end.
Bonjour! Ah, you look like someone who is about to travel. Have you a gas lamp left burning at home? I did, all the way round the world!

Impey Barbicane, president of the Gun Club of Baltimore, 1865: cool-headed, serious, a great artillery engineer with nothing to do since the war ended, who proposes to fire a shell to the Moon. He explains the sums plainly: the speed, the aim, the date.
Sir, the Gun Club has done with war. We propose a nobler target: the Moon.
Calculations! I live on them. Give me a number and I'll give you a cannon.

Michel Ardan, a bold, laughing Frenchman with a lion's mane of red hair, who telegraphs the Gun Club: 'Replace spherical shell by cylindro-conical projectile. Shall go inside.' Afraid of nothing, wonderful company.
Why fire an empty shell? Make it hollow and I shall ride in it! Who's coming?
Dr Samuel Fergusson
A balloon cannot be steered, they say. Quite true. But the winds can be chosen, if one knows how to climb and sink.
Joe, Dr Fergusson's devoted, cheerful, nimble servant, who would follow the Doctor anywhere and has the sharpest eyes in the sky.
The Doctor's never been wrong yet. If he says we'll fly across Africa, we'll fly across Africa!
Robur the Conqueror

Robur, the engineer of the great flying ship Albatross, 1886: proud, fierce, certain that heavier-than-air machines will rule the sky and that balloons are toys. He scorns the Weldon Institute's balloon men but is generous to anyone who truly wants to learn to fly.
Balloons! Gas bags at the mercy of every breeze. The future belongs to the machine that is heavier than air. Come aboard the Albatross, and see.

Uncle Prudent, president of the Weldon Institute of Philadelphia, a club of balloon enthusiasts: stubborn, argumentative, sure the future is the great steerable balloon, and still cross that Robur carried him off in the Albatross.
Welcome to the Weldon Institute, where the lighter-than-air is honoured. Pay no attention to that fellow on the mast.

Captain Nemo of the Nautilus, 1868: proud, grave, learned, a lover of the sea and of music and science, who has cut himself off from the land for reasons he will not tell. Courteous to guests. His motto is 'Mobilis in mobili', moving in the moving element. He knows every reef and creature of the oceans, and speaks of them with deep feeling.
Welcome aboard the Nautilus. The sea is everything. It covers seven tenths of the globe. Here, one is free.

Pierre Aronnax, professor at the Paris Museum of Natural History, the narrator of Twenty Thousand Leagues: amazed by everything, eager to name every fish and coral, torn between wonder at Nemo's ship and the wish to go home.
Every fish, every coral, I note them all! What a laboratory this ocean is.
Conseil, Professor Aronnax's calm, loyal Flemish servant, who can classify any creature by class, order and family but cannot tell one fish from another by sight. Always says 'if master pleases'.
If master pleases, I can tell you the class, order and family of anything that swims past.
Ned Land, the hot-tempered Canadian master harpooner, the best there is, who wants land under his feet, fresh meat, and to get off the Nautilus as soon as he can.
A fine boat, sure. But a man needs land under his feet. Keep your eyes open, friend.

Cyrus Smith, the engineer, 1865: calm, practical, a Union officer who escaped from Richmond by balloon. He believes knowledge is the greatest tool, and he can make almost anything from what nature gives: fire, bricks, iron, glass, a telegraph. He teaches as he works, and never gives up.
We have nothing, you say? We have our hands, our heads, and an island. That is a great deal. Let us begin.
Pencroft, the sailor: brave, warm-hearted, quick to grumble and quick to laugh, devoted to young Herbert, mad for tobacco, and convinced Mr Smith can do anything at all.
Mr Smith'll get us out of this, you'll see. He'll make fire out of nothing and a ship out of a tree!
Herbert Brown, fifteen, the sailor Pencroft's ward: a keen young naturalist who knows plants and animals from his books, brave and kind.
Look at the birds here! I've never seen half of them. This island is a whole natural-history book.
Gideon Spilett, war correspondent of the New York Herald: cool, fearless, a fine shot and an even finer note-taker, who writes down everything that happens on the island.
I've reported on battles, but this beats them all. Every page of my notebook is a wonder.
Neb (Nebuchadnezzar), Cyrus Smith's devoted friend: free-born, brave, a fine cook and tireless worker, who searched the shore for days when Mr Smith was lost in the sea.
Mr Cyrus came through the sea and the storm. Nothing on this island will stop him, nor us.

Professor Otto Lidenbrock of Hamburg, 1863, professor of mineralogy: impatient, explosive, tremendously learned, determined to follow the old alchemist Arne Saknussemm's path to the centre of the Earth, and quite unable to believe anything could stop him.
Saknussemm went down. So shall we! Axel, the ropes! Hans, the lamps!
Axel, the Professor's young nephew, the narrator: nervous, honest, in love with Graüben back in Hamburg, frightened of the whole idea, and yet he sees every wonder of the journey and tells it.
My uncle means it. He truly means to go down there. Tell me I'm dreaming.

Hans Bjelke, the Icelandic eider-down hunter who guides the Professor and Axel: tall, silent, utterly calm, strong and kind, who says very little and saves their lives again and again. He is paid every Saturday, three rix-dollars, wherever he is.
Hvad behöves? ...He means: what is needed? Hans says little. He does much.
The pearl diver of Ceylon

A poor pearl diver of the Gulf of Mannar, off Ceylon, saved from a shark by Captain Nemo, who gave him a bag of pearls. He tells you the strange captain comes to these waters, then goes away south and east, where there is a far reef with a curtain of black coral that no diver dares.
The man with the iron boat saved me from the shark. He gave me pearls. He goes to a far reef, they say, where the black coral grows like a curtain.

Jup (Master Jupiter), the orangutan who lives with the castaways in Granite House: clever, gentle, helpful, a fine waiter at table and fond of a little cake. He answers only with friendly grunts and gestures, never words.

Captain Nemo · Mobilis in Mobili
a sailor of the Mongolia

A cheerful English sailor of the P&O steamer Mongolia, which runs from Brindisi to Bombay through the new Suez Canal (opened 1869). He talks about coaling stations, the canal, the heat of the Red Sea, and a strange gentleman who timed the voyage to the minute.
a porter of the quay
An old porter of the quay who has carried trunks for every kind of traveller: explorers, balloonists, a professor with a box of rock samples. He thinks they're all mad and loves them for it.
a visitor to the Exposition

A visitor to the Exposition of Extraordinary Voyages, 1870, amazed by the iron-and-glass Palace, the electric lamps and the models of flying machines and submarines. She has a guidebook and an opinion about everything in it.
a newspaper seller
A newspaper seller shouting the headlines of 1870: a monster sighted at sea (which some say is a submarine), the Gun Club's latest scheme, the new railway across America. Cheeky and well-informed.
a balloon-field hand
A rigger at the balloon field who checks every rope of the Victoria. He explains how hydrogen lifts a balloon and why you must never strike a match near one.
A foundryman of the Exposition foundry, black with soot and proud of it. He talks about casting iron and bronze, steam hammers and the great cannon cast in Florida.
Good day! Here for the Exposition?
⚓ The harbour master's boats A steam launch leaves the quay every hour for the islands. You can sail it yourself, too, from the jetty (or swim, if you are brave).
🏝️ To Lincoln Island (the south beach)
The Mysterious Island, west across the sea

🏝️ Lincoln Island. White surf, red granite cliffs to the east, and the volcano, Mount Franklin, always smoking over the green. The engineer and his friends are camped at the Chimneys , north-east along the shore under the cliffs.
🪨 To the Chimneys, under Granite House
Where Cyrus Smith and the castaways are
🪨 The Chimneys. A jumble of fallen granite at the foot of the cliff, where the castaways shelter. Cyrus Smith is here.
The little volcano island in the bay, where the Underground comes out
🌋 Stromboli. A cone of black ash, smoking gently. Somewhere deep under it, the Underground opens up.

The sea cave east of the harbour
🌊 The Nautilus dock. The submarine lies at her mooring in the cave, lit from below. Go aboard from the jetty.

North to Stapi, at the foot of Snaefells
Iceland: the turf village, Professor Lidenbrock, and the volcano
🌋 Stapi, under Snaefells. Turf houses, black lava, the cold sea wind. The snow-capped volcano rises to the north. Professor Lidenbrock is at the pastor's house, impatient to climb.
East to Stone's Hill, Florida
The Columbiad, the Moon gun
🌕 Stone's Hill, Florida. A plain of sand and scrub, a ring of furnaces round a great stone collar in the ground: the mouth of the Columbiad, nine hundred feet deep.

Everything here is Safe except the Deep, the Underground beyond the camp at Port Graüben, and Lincoln Island's Far West jungle and Serpentine Peninsula.
Out under the iron and glass, onto the square.

🏛️ The Palace of the Exposition. Under a vault of glass a hundred and eighty metres long: models of every machine in the Voyages, electric lamps, and in the middle the Inventors' Hall , four great design benches where you build a machine of your own and test it for real.
The Nautilus (a model)

Captain Nemo's submarine, 70 metres long, of steel plates over a double hull, driven by electricity from sodium batteries. Aronnax calls her 'a masterpiece of industry'. Real submarines of 1870 (like the French Plongeur of 1863, which Verne saw a model of at the 1867 Paris Exposition) could barely dive at all.
The Columbiad's shell

An aluminium projectile 9 feet wide and 12 feet high, with padded walls, water-buffers against the shock, and windows. Verne chose aluminium because it was light and very new (it cost more than silver in 1865).

Robur's flying ship (Robur the Conqueror, 1886): a long hull with 37 masts of lifting screws and two propellers, driven by electric batteries. Heavier than air, as aeroplanes and helicopters are today.
From The Steam House (1880): a mechanical elephant drawing two houses on wheels across India. You can buy one of your own from the ship chandler on the quay.
